lessons.title: Something Strange at the Water Plant

quiz.prompt: Before the demonstration, a student writes: "Sodium will be safe in Lake Victoria water because we eat it every day in salt on our ugali." What is the main problem with this prediction?
choices: Sodium metal is only found in the sea, so it cannot be tested with lake water.
Salt is sodium chloride, a compound. Pure sodium metal is a different substance and can behave very differently.
Sodium is a gas, so it would escape from the water before reacting.
Sodium in salt and pure sodium metal are exactly the same, so the prediction is correct but badly explained.
quiz.rationale: The common misconception is to confuse the compound (sodium chloride) with the element (sodium metal). The two are different substances with different properties.
quiz.placement: Predict: Mystery Substance Card (A: sodium chloride, B: sodium metal), prompt 1

quiz.prompt: In the demonstration, each substance was placed in cold water. Which row correctly describes what was observed?
choices: Sodium, magnesium and aluminium: all fizz in the same way. Argon: no change.
Sodium: barely fizzes. Magnesium: skims and burns with an orange flame. Aluminium: fizzes slowly. Argon: dissolves.
Sodium: skims and fizzes with an orange flame. Magnesium: barely fizzes. Aluminium: no visible reaction. Argon: no change.
Sodium: no reaction. Magnesium: violent fizzing. Aluminium: a few bubbles. Argon: orange flame.
quiz.rationale: Sodium reacts violently, magnesium shows only a few tiny bubbles, aluminium shows no visible change and argon shows no change. This tests the left-to-right pattern across Period 3 that the students saw.
quiz.placement: Observe: live demonstration or video of sodium, magnesium, aluminium and argon (Observation Table)

quiz.prompt: A drop of phenolphthalein indicator was added to the water after sodium reacted with it. The solution turned pink. What can students conclude from this observation?
choices: The solution has become acidic.
The solution is still neutral, the same as the original water.
The solution has become alkaline.
The solution has become very hot, and heat turns phenolphthalein pink.
quiz.rationale: Phenolphthalein turns pink in alkaline solutions. The lesson says sodium leaves behind a strongly alkaline solution. Why this happens is not explained yet.
quiz.placement: Observe: sodium dropped into water, solution turns phenolphthalein pink

quiz.prompt: Students filled in an Observation Table while watching sodium react with water. Which entry belongs in the "What I Infer" column, because it is an inference and not a direct observation?
choices: The flame was orange.
A gas is being produced.
The solution turned pink after the indicator was added.
The sodium skimmed across the surface of the water.
quiz.rationale: Skimming, flame colour and the pink colour can all be seen directly. A gas being made is a guess based on the fizzing, so it is an inference.
quiz.placement: Observe: structured Observation Table (What I See | What I Hear | What I Infer)

quiz.prompt: In the class demonstration, potassium reacted with water more violently than sodium, and sodium reacted more violently than lithium. A chef in Mombasa drops a small piece of lithium into a pot of water. Based on this pattern in Group I, how will the reaction compare with the sodium reaction the class watched?
choices: It will be more violent, because lithium is higher up the group.
It will be less violent, because reactivity increases going down Group I and lithium is above sodium.
It will be more violent, because lithium is lighter than sodium.
It will be exactly the same, because lithium and sodium are in the same group.
quiz.rationale: Reactivity with water increases down Group I (Li < Na < K). Lithium sits above sodium, so it reacts less violently. The option about "lighter" reflects the misconception named in the lesson.
quiz.placement: Explain: Group I Physical Properties data sheet, question 3 (lithium in the chef's pot)

quiz.prompt: Sodium and magnesium are neighbours in Period 3, but sodium reacts violently with cold water and magnesium barely reacts. At the end of Lesson 1, which statement about WHY they differ is most accurate?
choices: Both are metals, so they should react in the same way and the difference must be a mistake.
Sodium reacts more violently because it is found in salt.
The class has only observed the difference so far. The reason is still an open question to investigate in later lessons.
Magnesium is not a metal, so it cannot react like sodium.
quiz.rationale: This is the anchor lesson. Students record the puzzle on the Driving Question Board and have not yet been taught a reason. Magnesium is a metal, and the salt idea is a misconception.
quiz.placement: DQB: Driving Question Board (YELLOW notes: what I want to know to understand the sodium explosion)

quiz.prompt: Argon sits right next to chlorine on the periodic table. When the class was told what happens if argon is tapped, shaken or has a flame held near it, what was the result?
choices: It reacts slowly with a few bubbles, like magnesium.
It reacts like chlorine because they are neighbours.
It burns with an orange flame, like sodium.
Nothing happens. Argon shows no change at all.
quiz.rationale: Argon is completely inert and shows no change. Being next to a reactive element does not make an element reactive, so the pattern reverses at the noble gases.
quiz.placement: Observe: argon ampoule photograph or video (end-of-lesson recap of Period 3 pattern)

quiz.prompt: A teacher holds an inverted test tube over lithium reacting with cold water and then puts a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube. The splint goes out with a squeaky pop. Which gas has been collected?
choices: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen
Steam
quiz.rationale: Group I metals react with cold water to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when tested with a lighted splint.
quiz.placement: Stage 1: Lithium with water (teacher demonstration), testing the gas with a lighted splint

quiz.prompt: Three drops of universal indicator are added to the water in a trough. A small piece of lithium reacts completely with the water. What will the indicator show about the final solution?
choices: It stays green because the solution is neutral
It does not change colour because lithium does not dissolve
It turns red because hydrogen gas makes the solution acidic
It turns blue or purple because the solution is alkaline
quiz.rationale: Lithium reacts with water to form lithium hydroxide, which dissolves to make an alkaline solution. Universal indicator shows blue or purple (high pH) in an alkali.
quiz.placement: Stage 1: Lithium with water, recording the colour change of the indicator and pH of the solution

quiz.prompt: Potassium is stored under oil in the laboratory. What is the main reason for this?
choices: It reacts with moisture in the air, so the oil keeps air and water away
The oil stops it from becoming a non-metal
The oil keeps it cool because it melts at room temperature
Potassium dissolves in oil and this makes it safe to carry
quiz.rationale: Potassium is so reactive that even moisture in the air begins to react with it. Storing it under oil keeps air and water away from the metal.
quiz.placement: Stage 3: Potassium with water (teacher demonstration only), safety narration about storage under oil

quiz.prompt: The electron arrangements are Li (2,1), Na (2,8,1) and K (2,8,8,1). What do all three atoms have in common?
choices: One electron in the outermost shell
The same number of electron shells
The same number of protons in the nucleus
The same total number of electrons
quiz.rationale: Each atom ends with a 1 in its electron arrangement, so each has one outer-shell electron. This is the electron they lose when they react. The number of shells, protons and total electrons all differ.
quiz.placement: Activity 1: Electron configuration diagrams for Li, Na and K

quiz.prompt: The first ionisation energy of lithium is 520 kJ/mol and that of potassium is 419 kJ/mol. How much less energy (in kJ/mol) is needed to remove the outer electron from potassium than from lithium?
quiz.rationale: Subtract the values: 520 - 419 = 101 kJ/mol. Less energy is needed for potassium, so it loses its outer electron more easily and is more reactive.
quiz.placement: Activity 2: Linking configuration to ionisation energy (bar chart of Li, Na, K data strip card)

quiz.prompt: A learner writes the caption: 'Reactivity increases down Group I because potassium has more protons than lithium, so it holds its electron more tightly.' Which statement best corrects this idea?
choices: Going down the group, atoms become heavier, so they move faster in water
Going down the group, the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so it is lost more easily
Going down the group, atoms gain more outer electrons, so they react more
Going down the group, ionisation energy increases, so the outer electron is lost more easily
quiz.rationale: More shells place the outer electron further away and increase shielding. This reduces the pull of the nucleus, lowers ionisation energy and makes the electron easier to lose. The learner's statement about protons is a misconception because the extra distance and shielding outweigh the extra protons.
quiz.placement: Model Sketch: caption 'Reactivity increases down Group I because...'

quiz.prompt: Which equation correctly represents the reaction of sodium with cold water, with balancing and state symbols?
choices: 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + 2H2(g)
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + O2(g)
Na(s) + H2O(l) → NaOH(aq) + H2(g)
quiz.rationale: Sodium and water give sodium hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas. Counting atoms: 2 Na, 4 H and 2 O on each side. The other equations are unbalanced or give the wrong gas.
quiz.placement: Activity 3: Writing balanced equations with state symbols (peer-check)

lessons.title: Magnesium, Calcium and the Stubborn Metals

quiz.prompt: A student places a 3 cm strip of pre-cleaned magnesium ribbon into a test tube of cold water and watches it for 5 minutes. Which observation is most likely?
choices: The ribbon skims across the water and burns with an orange flame, like sodium
The ribbon stays completely unchanged, like aluminium, with no gas at all
The ribbon fizzes so vigorously that it dissolves within seconds
Only a few slow bubbles form over several minutes, and the solution turns slightly alkaline
quiz.rationale: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water, giving a few slow hydrogen bubbles and a weakly alkaline solution of magnesium hydroxide. It is much less vigorous than sodium.
quiz.placement: Investigation A — Magnesium in Cold Water

quiz.prompt: A teacher drops a small piece of calcium into cold water and the class compares it with magnesium in cold water and sodium in cold water. Which ranking, from MOST vigorous to LEAST vigorous, is correct?
choices: Sodium, calcium, magnesium
Magnesium, calcium, sodium
Calcium, sodium, magnesium
Sodium, magnesium, calcium
quiz.rationale: Sodium is the most vigorous of all. Calcium reacts faster than magnesium but less violently than sodium, and magnesium is the slowest in cold water.
quiz.placement: Teacher demonstration — Calcium in Cold Water, and the ranking of reactions with sodium placed in the ranking

quiz.prompt: Going down Group II from beryllium to barium, which pair of trends is correct?
choices: Atomic radius increases and first ionisation energy increases
Atomic radius decreases and first ionisation energy decreases
Atomic radius increases and first ionisation energy decreases
Atomic radius decreases and first ionisation energy increases
quiz.rationale: Each element down the group has an extra electron shell, so atoms get bigger. The outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and easier to remove, so first ionisation energy falls.
quiz.placement: Graphing task — atomic radius and first ionisation energy graphs down Group II

quiz.prompt: The melting points of Group II metals are: Be 1287 °C, Mg 650 °C, Ca 842 °C, Sr 777 °C, Ba 727 °C. Which statement describes the trend correctly?
choices: Melting point increases steadily from Be to Ba
Melting point decreases smoothly with every element lower than the one before
Melting point stays about the same for all Group II metals
Melting point decreases overall from Be to Ba, but not smoothly, because calcium is higher than magnesium
quiz.rationale: The overall trend is a decrease from 1287 °C to 727 °C. Calcium (842 °C) is higher than magnesium (650 °C), so the fall is not smooth.
quiz.placement: Graphing task — melting point graph and circling the exception at calcium

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct balanced equation for magnesium reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid?
choices: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l)
Mg(s) + HCl(aq) → MgCl(aq) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H(g)
quiz.rationale: Magnesium forms Mg²⁺, so it needs two chloride ions (MgCl₂). Hydrogen is released as the diatomic gas H₂, and both sides have 1 Mg, 2 H and 2 Cl.
quiz.placement: Writing balanced chemical equations for each reaction observed (dilute acid)

quiz.prompt: Sodium (2,8,1) and magnesium (2,8,2) are neighbours in Period 3. Which statement best explains why magnesium is less reactive than sodium with cold water?
choices: Magnesium has only one outer electron, so there is less to lose
Magnesium has fewer protons than sodium, so it holds its electrons less strongly
Magnesium atoms must lose two electrons, and its outer electrons are held more strongly by a greater nuclear charge, giving a higher ionisation energy
Magnesium has one more electron shell than sodium, so its outer electron is shielded more
quiz.rationale: Magnesium has one more proton in the same number of shells, so its outer electrons are pulled harder and it must lose two electrons. This gives a higher ionisation energy and less reactivity than sodium.
quiz.placement: Two-Electron Tax sensemaking frame — Na and Mg electron configuration comparison

quiz.prompt: Calcium (2,8,8,2) reacts more vigorously with cold water than magnesium (2,8,2), even though calcium has more protons. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Calcium has fewer outer electrons than magnesium, so it loses them more easily
Calcium has more protons, so it pulls its outer electrons more strongly and loses them more easily
Calcium has a higher first ionisation energy than magnesium, so it reacts faster
Calcium has more inner shells, so more shielding and a greater distance from the nucleus make its outer electrons easier to remove
quiz.rationale: Down the group, extra inner shells increase shielding and distance, which outweighs the extra protons. Outer electrons are lost more easily (lower ionisation energy), so reactivity increases.
quiz.placement: Three-sentence explanation: going from magnesium to calcium down Group II, reactivity increases because…

quiz.prompt: Which electron arrangement is correct for a calcium atom (atomic number 20)?
quiz.rationale: Calcium has 20 electrons, arranged 2, 8, 8, 2. It has two outer electrons and three filled inner shells, as for other Group II elements.
quiz.placement: Task 1 — Add Magnesium and Calcium to the electron-shell model diagram

lessons.title: The Halogen Family: From Gas to Solid

quiz.prompt: In Group I, reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is lost more easily from a larger atom. A learner predicts that reactivity in Group VII will also increase down the group, using the same reasoning. What is wrong with this prediction?
choices: Halogens have no outer electrons, so their reactivity cannot be predicted from electron shells
Halogen atoms get smaller down the group, so they hold electrons more tightly and become more reactive
Group VII elements do not change in reactivity because they all have seven outer electrons
Halogens react by gaining an electron, and in a larger atom with more shielding the nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly, so reactivity is expected to decrease
quiz.rationale: Group I atoms lose electrons, so more shielding makes reaction easier. Halogens gain electrons, so more shielding and a larger radius make it harder to attract the incoming electron, and reactivity falls down the group.
quiz.placement: Think-Pair-Share: predicting whether Group VII reactivity increases, stays the same or decreases down the group

quiz.prompt: Which row correctly describes chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature?
choices: Chlorine: grey-black solid; bromine: orange-brown liquid; iodine: yellow-green gas
Chlorine: yellow-green gas; bromine: orange-brown liquid; iodine: grey-black solid
Chlorine: orange-brown liquid; bromine: yellow-green gas; iodine: grey-black solid
Chlorine: yellow-green gas; bromine: grey-black solid; iodine: orange-brown liquid
quiz.rationale: Going down Group VII the physical state changes from gas (Cl₂) to liquid (Br₂) to solid (I₂), and the colour gets darker. Iodine is a grey-black solid that gives off violet vapour.
quiz.placement: Part A: Physical Properties Carousel (observation table of colour and physical state)

quiz.prompt: Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution, then 1 cm³ of cyclohexane is added and the tube is shaken. The cyclohexane layer turns orange-brown. What substance has formed in that layer?
choices: Bromine, Br₂, which was displaced from the bromide ions by chlorine
Potassium chloride, KCl, which dissolves in cyclohexane
Chlorine, Cl₂, which dissolved in the cyclohexane
Iodine, I₂, which was released from the solution
quiz.rationale: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from potassium bromide: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. The orange-brown colour in the organic layer is the bromine.
quiz.placement: Part B, Demo 3: Displacement 1 (Cl₂ displacing Br⁻) with cyclohexane

quiz.prompt: Chlorine can displace bromide ions, and bromine can displace iodide ions. A learner adds iodine solution to potassium chloride solution. What is expected?
choices: Iodine displaces chlorine, forming chlorine gas and potassium iodide
Iodine displaces chlorine because iodine atoms are the largest
A violent reaction, because iodine is the most reactive halogen
No displacement, because iodine is less reactive than chlorine and cannot displace chloride ions
quiz.rationale: A halogen displaces only the halide of a less reactive halogen. Iodine is the weakest oxidising agent of the three, so it cannot displace chloride ions.
quiz.placement: Part B, after Demo 4: prediction 'Can I₂ displace Cl⁻?'

quiz.prompt: The energy released when each atom gains one electron is: chlorine 349 kJ/mol, bromine 325 kJ/mol, iodine 295 kJ/mol. What does this data show about reactivity?
choices: Iodine is the most reactive because it has the lowest electron affinity
Chlorine is the most reactive because it releases the most energy when gaining an electron, so it attracts an incoming electron most strongly
Bromine is the most reactive because its value is in the middle
All three are equally reactive because they each gain one electron
quiz.rationale: Chlorine has the highest electron affinity (349 kJ/mol), so it gains an electron most easily and is the most reactive of the three. Electron affinity falls to iodine as the atoms get larger and more shielded.
quiz.placement: Part A: Constructing the Explanation using the Electron Affinity Scaffold Card

quiz.prompt: Which equation for the reaction of iron with chlorine gas is correctly balanced?
choices: Fe + Cl₂ → FeCl₃
2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃
Fe + 3Cl₂ → FeCl₃
2Fe + 2Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃
quiz.rationale: Iron(III) chloride is FeCl₃. Two FeCl₃ need 2 Fe and 6 Cl atoms, which is 3 Cl₂ molecules, so 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃ balances.
quiz.placement: Part C: Equations Practice (balanced equation for iron wool and chlorine)

quiz.prompt: The water officer in Kisumu uses chlorine, not bromine or iodine, to treat Lake Victoria water. Which statement gives the best scientific reason from this lesson?
choices: Chlorine is the strongest oxidising agent of the three because it has the highest electron affinity, and it is also cheap and easy to supply
Chlorine is the only halogen that reacts with metals
Iodine is too reactive to be used safely in water
Bromine has the smallest atoms of the three, so it is the weakest oxidising agent
quiz.rationale: Reactivity and oxidising power decrease from Cl to Br to I, so chlorine is the strongest oxidising agent of the three. Cost and easy supply are also practical reasons. Iodine is the least reactive, not the most.
quiz.placement: DQB bridge statement: why the water officer uses CHLORINE (not bromine or iodine)

quiz.prompt: A learner adds a Group VII panel to the class model with a reactivity arrow for Cl, Br and I. Which arrow is correct?
choices: An arrow pointing down, because reactivity increases down every group
An arrow pointing down, because iodine has the largest atom and attracts electrons best
No arrow, because all halogens are equally reactive
An arrow pointing up, because chlorine at the top is the most reactive and the strongest oxidising agent
quiz.rationale: In Group VII reactivity decreases down the group, so the arrow points upward towards chlorine. This is the reverse of Group I, where the reactivity arrow points downward.
quiz.placement: Model Building: adding the Group VII panel (reactivity arrow) to the class cumulative model poster

lessons.title: The Nobles and the Patterns of Eight

quiz.prompt: A water purification officer stored sodium inside a sealed ampoule of argon gas. Which statement best explains why argon was a safe choice?
choices: Argon has one outer electron that it holds very tightly
Argon has 7 outer electrons, so it only reacts with metals that are not very reactive
Argon has a full outer shell of 8 electrons, so it does not need to lose, gain or share electrons
Argon has no electrons, so it cannot react with anything
quiz.rationale: Argon is 2,8,8, so its outer shell is full. This stable arrangement makes it chemically inert, so it will not react with the reactive sodium.
quiz.placement: Predict: students write why argon was chosen to protect the sodium

quiz.prompt: The boiling points of the Group VIII elements are: helium −269 °C, neon −246 °C, argon −186 °C, krypton −153 °C. Which statement best explains this trend down the group?
choices: The atoms get smaller down the group, so they pack together more tightly
The covalent bonds inside each atom get stronger down the group
The atoms lose outer electrons more easily down the group, so they attract each other more
The atoms get larger and have more electrons, so the London dispersion forces between atoms get stronger
quiz.rationale: Atomic radius and electron number increase down Group VIII, so the London dispersion forces between atoms get stronger. More energy is needed to separate the atoms, so the boiling point rises.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Group VIII data table analysis (Q1, boiling point trend)

quiz.prompt: Across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine, atomic radius decreases. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The atoms lose electrons across the period, so they become smaller
The number of protons decreases, so the nucleus pulls less on the outer electrons
Each element has fewer electron shells than the one before it
The nuclear charge increases while the number of shells stays the same and shielding is almost constant, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly
quiz.rationale: Each step across Period 3 adds one proton, but the electrons go into the same outer shell. Shielding stays nearly constant, so the stronger nuclear attraction pulls the outer electrons closer.
quiz.placement: Activity B: Period 3 graph-plotting relay (Group B: atomic radius graph)

quiz.prompt: When the melting points of Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl and Ar are plotted against atomic number, silicon has by far the highest melting point. Why?
choices: Silicon has a giant covalent structure, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it
Silicon has the weakest London dispersion forces in Period 3
Silicon has the largest atoms in Period 3, so it has the strongest forces between them
Silicon is the most metallic element in Period 3
quiz.rationale: Silicon has a giant covalent structure in which every atom is joined to others by strong covalent bonds. A large amount of energy is needed to break these bonds, so the melting point peaks at silicon.
quiz.placement: Activity B: Period 3 graph-plotting relay (Group C: melting point graph)

quiz.prompt: The first ionisation energy of aluminium (2,8,3) is lower than that of magnesium (2,8,2). Which statement best explains this dip?
choices: Aluminium has fewer protons than magnesium
Aluminium's outer electrons are paired and repel each other
Aluminium's outer electron is in a 3p sub-shell, which is slightly higher in energy than the 3s sub-shell, so it is easier to remove
Aluminium has a full outer shell, so it does not hold its electrons tightly
quiz.rationale: Magnesium's two outer electrons are in the 3s sub-shell. Aluminium's third outer electron is in a higher-energy 3p sub-shell, so it is removed more easily and the ionisation energy dips.
quiz.placement: Part A: Gallery Walk + Anomaly Explanation (ionisation energy dip at Al)

quiz.prompt: Sulfur (2,8,6) has a lower first ionisation energy than phosphorus (2,8,5). Which statement best explains this dip?
choices: In sulfur, two electrons are paired in one 3p orbital and repel each other, so one is easier to remove
Sulfur has a full 3p sub-shell, which makes it unstable
Sulfur's outer electron is in the 4s sub-shell, which is further from the nucleus
Sulfur has fewer protons than phosphorus
quiz.rationale: Phosphorus has one electron in each 3p orbital. Sulfur must pair two electrons in one 3p orbital, and the repulsion between them makes one easier to remove.
quiz.placement: Part A: Gallery Walk + Anomaly Explanation (ionisation energy dip at S)

quiz.prompt: Mama Achieng's aluminium sufuria conducts better than a piece of sodium. Which statement best explains why the conductivity of the metals increases from Na to Mg to Al?
choices: Aluminium atoms have more electron shells than sodium atoms
The number of delocalised electrons per atom increases (Na: 1, Mg: 2, Al: 3)
Sodium atoms are heavier than aluminium atoms
Aluminium atoms lose electrons less easily than sodium atoms, so they hold the current inside
quiz.rationale: Each Na atom gives 1 delocalised electron, each Mg atom 2 and each Al atom 3. More delocalised electrons per atom means a higher electron density and better conductivity.
quiz.placement: Part B: Conductivity and Physical Properties of Period 3 Metals

quiz.prompt: Sodium conducts electricity less well than aluminium, yet sodium reacts far more violently with water. Which property is the better predictor of how reactive a metal is with water?
choices: Electrical conductivity, because it shows how many electrons a metal has
Electrical conductivity, because a better conductor reacts faster
Ionisation energy, because a low value means an electron is lost easily, so the metal is more reactive
Melting point, because metals with high melting points react fastest
quiz.rationale: Metals react with water by losing electrons, so a low ionisation energy means higher reactivity. Conductivity and reactivity measure different things.
quiz.placement: Part B: 2-sentence answer on ionisation energy versus conductivity as a predictor of reactivity

quiz.prompt: Chlorine is right next to argon in Period 3. Why was argon, and not chlorine, used to protect the sodium?
choices: Chlorine has a higher first ionisation energy than argon, so it would react with sodium
Argon has 7 outer electrons, so it gains an electron from sodium more easily than chlorine does
Chlorine has a full outer shell, so it would react more strongly than argon
Chlorine has 7 outer electrons and readily gains an electron, so it would react violently with sodium, while argon's full outer shell of 8 makes it inert
quiz.rationale: Chlorine is reactive because it gains one electron to complete its outer shell, so it would react with sodium. Argon already has a full outer shell of 8 electrons and reacts with nothing.
quiz.placement: Model: stability scale and the argon-versus-chlorine test question

lessons.title: Period 3 Reacts: Metals, Non-Metals and the Chlorine Test

quiz.prompt: The first ionisation energies of four period 3 elements are: Na 496 kJ/mol, Mg 738 kJ/mol, Al 578 kJ/mol, Si 786 kJ/mol. Using only this data, which element would you predict to lose its outer electron most easily and so react most vigorously with cold water?
choices: Magnesium, because it has two outer electrons to give away
Silicon, because it has the highest ionisation energy
Sodium, because it has the lowest ionisation energy
Aluminium, because it has the highest nuclear charge of the three metals
quiz.rationale: The lowest ionisation energy (496 kJ/mol) means the outer electron is removed most easily, so sodium forms its ion and reacts most vigorously.
quiz.placement: Predict: POE worksheet predictions using the Lesson 5 ionisation energy bar chart

quiz.prompt: A water officer drops a small piece of sodium into a beaker of water. It skims across the surface, fizzes and burns with an orange flame. After the reaction stops, what is left in the beaker?
choices: Pure water with solid sodium at the bottom
A neutral solution of sodium chloride
A strongly acidic solution
A strongly alkaline solution
quiz.rationale: Sodium reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas. Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali, so the solution is strongly alkaline.
quiz.placement: Observe: Na in water teacher demonstration behind the safety screen

quiz.prompt: A strip of aluminium foil placed in dilute hydrochloric acid reacts very slowly at first, and more slowly than magnesium does. What is the main reason for the slow start?
choices: Aluminium is a non-metal, so it cannot react with acids
Aluminium has more outer electrons than magnesium, so it needs more acid
A thin oxide film on the aluminium surface must be removed before the acid reaches the metal
Aluminium has fewer protons than magnesium, so it holds its electrons more weakly
quiz.rationale: Aluminium is covered by a thin, protective aluminium oxide film. The acid has to break through this film before the metal underneath can react.
quiz.placement: Observe: Al foil in dilute HCl compared with Mg from Lesson 3

quiz.prompt: Sulfur burns in oxygen to give a colourful flame and a gas with a sharp smell. Which statement about this product is correct?
choices: It is sulfur dioxide, a basic oxide
It is sodium sulfide, a neutral solid
It is sulfur dioxide, an acidic oxide
It is hydrogen sulfide, an acidic gas
quiz.rationale: Sulfur is a non-metal, and non-metals form acidic oxides. Burning sulfur in oxygen gives sulfur dioxide, the sharp-smelling gas, which is acidic.
quiz.placement: Observe: sulfur burning in oxygen (fume cupboard demonstration or video)

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct balanced equation, with state symbols, for magnesium reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid?
choices: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl(aq) + H2(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + 2H(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
Mg(s) + HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
quiz.rationale: Magnesium chloride is MgCl2, and hydrogen is released as H2 gas. Counting atoms, 1 Mg, 2 H and 2 Cl on each side shows the equation is balanced.
quiz.placement: Explain: Task A, balanced equation for Mg(s) + HCl(aq) with peer checking

quiz.prompt: Magnesium has two outer electrons and sodium has only one, yet magnesium reacts much more slowly with water than sodium does. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Magnesium has 12 protons against 11 in sodium, with similar shielding, so it holds its outer electrons more tightly
Magnesium has a larger atomic mass, so it moves more slowly in water
Magnesium has more electrons, so it has much more shielding than sodium
Two outer electrons are always easier to remove than one
quiz.rationale: Across period 3 the nuclear charge increases while shielding stays almost constant. Magnesium's outer electrons are held more strongly, so its ionisation energy is higher and it loses them less easily than sodium.
quiz.placement: Explain: Task B, electron configuration diagrams for Na, Mg, Al and Si and the nuclear charge vs shielding argument

quiz.prompt: A student draws a trend arrow across period 3 from Na to Al on an annotated periodic table. Which label is correct for the metals Na, Mg and Al?
choices: Reactivity with water stays the same because all three are metals
Reactivity with water increases from Na to Al as the nuclear charge increases
Reactivity with water decreases from Na to Al as ionisation energy generally increases
Reactivity with water decreases from Na to Al because shielding increases sharply
quiz.rationale: Nuclear charge increases with almost constant shielding, so ionisation energy generally rises. The outer electrons are then harder to remove and the metals react less readily with water from Na to Al.
quiz.placement: Model Building: trend arrow on the cumulative annotated periodic table for period 3

lessons.title: What Are These Elements Good For? — Uses, Applications & Final Explanation

quiz.prompt: A water purification officer in Kisumu drops sodium into Lake Victoria water and it reacts violently. A strip of magnesium, which is the next element in Period 3, barely fizzes in cold water. Which statement best explains why sodium is so much more reactive?
choices: Sodium has one outer electron, which is lost easily because sodium has a lower ionisation energy than magnesium
Sodium has two outer electrons, which makes it lose them more easily than magnesium
Sodium has more protons than magnesium, so it holds its outer electron more strongly
Sodium has a full outer shell, so it reacts more easily
quiz.rationale: Sodium (2,8,1) has one valence electron and a lower ionisation energy than magnesium (2,8,2). It loses that electron easily, so it reacts violently with water. Magnesium has more protons, not fewer, which holds its electrons more strongly.
quiz.placement: Predict: re-reading the Kisumu sodium-water demonstration and comparing with the Lesson 1 initial model

quiz.prompt: Welders on construction sites such as the SGR use argon gas to shield hot metal from the air. Why is argon suitable for this use?
choices: Argon has one outer electron that it gives away easily
Argon has a full outer shell of electrons, so it does not react with anything
Argon is a very reactive gas that quickly reacts with oxygen before the metal can
Argon needs one more electron to complete its outer shell, so it attracts electrons strongly
quiz.rationale: Argon (2,8,8) has a full outer shell, so it neither loses, gains nor shares electrons. It is inert and cannot react with the hot metal.
quiz.placement: Group D presentation: Group VIII elements (argon as inert shielding gas in welding)

quiz.prompt: Chlorine is added to Lake Victoria water at a treatment plant in Kisumu to kill bacteria. Which property of chlorine, linked to its electron configuration, makes it effective?
choices: It has one outer electron that it loses easily, so it is a strong reducing agent
It has a full outer shell, so it is completely inert
It has a very large atomic size, so it is easily pulled apart by bacteria
It has 7 outer electrons and a high electronegativity, so it strongly pulls electrons from other substances (it is a strong oxidising agent)
quiz.rationale: Chlorine (2,8,7) needs only one more electron to fill its outer shell. This gives it high electronegativity and strong oxidising power, so it damages bacterial cells.
quiz.placement: Group C presentation: Group VII elements (chlorine in water treatment at a plant such as the one in Kisumu)

quiz.prompt: Cement used in Kenyan construction is made from calcium compounds such as limestone (CaCO₃). Calcium atoms form Ca²⁺ ions in these compounds. What does the 2+ charge tell us about calcium?
choices: Calcium gains two electrons, so it has two outer electrons missing
Calcium has a full outer shell, so it forms ions without any change
Calcium has two outer electrons, which it loses to form the 2+ ion in its compounds
Calcium is present in cement as the pure metal, which is stable in air
quiz.rationale: Calcium is in Group II and has two valence electrons. It loses both to form Ca²⁺, so it is found in cement as compounds, not as the reactive metal.
quiz.placement: Group B presentation: Group II elements (calcium in cement production and teacher prompt on the form of calcium in cement)

quiz.prompt: Potassium explodes more violently in water than sodium, and sodium reacts more violently than lithium. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Going down Group I, the nuclear charge increases, so the outer electron is held more strongly and lost more easily
Going down Group I, the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily
Going down Group I, the outer shell becomes full, so the metals become more reactive
Going down Group I, the number of outer electrons increases, so more electrons are available to react
quiz.rationale: Down Group I there are more electron shells, so the single outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded. Its ionisation energy is lower, so it is lost more easily and reactivity increases.
quiz.placement: Whole-class synthesis: 'Why does potassium explode more violently than sodium, which explodes more violently than lithium?'

quiz.prompt: Going from left to right across Period 3 (Na to Ar), how does first ionisation energy change, and why?
choices: It decreases, because more electrons repel each other and are lost more easily
It generally increases, because the nuclear charge increases while the electrons are added to the same shell, so they are held more strongly
It increases, because more shells are added across the period
It stays the same, because all the elements are in the same period
quiz.rationale: Across a period the number of protons increases but the electrons go into the same shell, so shielding stays about the same. The outer electrons are pulled more strongly and ionisation energy generally increases. No new shells are added across a period.
quiz.placement: DQB closure: pairs answer Lesson 1 questions citing evidence (e.g. Lesson 5 ionisation energies across Period 3)

quiz.prompt: Sodium is in Period 3 and Group I. Which shows the number of electrons in each shell of a sodium atom?
quiz.rationale: Sodium has atomic number 11, so it has 11 electrons. They fill the shells as 2, 8, 1, giving 3 shells (Period 3) and 1 outer electron (Group I).
quiz.placement: Final Cumulative Annotated Periodic Table Model: annotating electron configurations for Li, Na, K, Mg, Ca, Cl, Br, I, Ar

quiz.prompt: Which statement is the best overall explanation for why elements such as sodium, magnesium, chlorine and argon behave so differently?
choices: Their reactivity depends only on how many protons each atom has
Elements in the same period react in the same way because they have the same number of shells
The position of an element in the periodic table shows its electron configuration, and the number of outer electrons, shielding and ionisation energy determine how it behaves
Their reactivity depends on the colour and state of the element
quiz.rationale: The unit's main idea is that position in the periodic table shows electron configuration. Together with shielding and ionisation energy, this determines how easily an element loses or gains electrons. Atomic number alone, or the number of shells alone, cannot explain the differences.
quiz.placement: Individual Final Explanation answering the driving question and the class consensus answer
